title: To the land of a just king
hook: the Prophet ﷺ sends some to Abyssinia, where a king rules who wrongs no one (sirah)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ta-Ha. Your line was: the page turned him. Which page did you read slowly, and what line in it surprised you? Day seven hundred forty-two.

A leader who can't protect his people has a hard choice. He can tell them to hold on. He can tell them to fight. Or he can tell them to leave. Ibn Ishaq says that when the Prophet, peace be upon him, saw what his companions were suffering, and saw that he could not shield them, he pointed them across the sea, to Abyssinia. His reason wasn't that the land was Muslim. It wasn't. His reason was the man who ruled it. Today: hijrah.
screen: `HOLD ON, FIGHT, OR LEAVE?` → `ACROSS THE SEA.` → `BECAUSE OF THE KING.`

segments.voice: Here is what Ibn Ishaq has him say, in paraphrase: if you go to Abyssinia, you'll find a king there under whom no one is wronged. It is a land of truthfulness, until God makes a way out for you from what you're in. Look at what he praises. Not the king's religion; he is a Christian, ruling a Christian land. Not his wealth or his army. Justice: in his land, no one is wronged. The Prophet trusted his people to a ruler of another faith because that ruler was fair. So some of the Muslims went. Ibn Ishaq calls it the first emigration in Islam, the first hijrah, before the later one to Medina. Among those who went, he names Uthman ibn Affan and his wife Ruqayyah, the Prophet's own daughter. This wasn't sending strangers away. He sent his child. And Umm Salamah, who went too, later remembered what they found. In the report kept in Musnad Ahmad, she says they came to the best of neighbors, that they were safe in their faith, and worshipped God without being harmed or hearing anything they hated. Safe in their faith, in someone else's country. The story doesn't end quietly; tomorrow, Quraysh come after them. But for now, notice the picture: the first hijrah was Muslims running for safety to the court of a just king.
screen: `NO ONE IS WRONGED THERE.` · `HE PRAISES JUSTICE, NOT RELIGION.` · `HE SENT HIS OWN DAUGHTER.` · `SAFE IN THEIR FAITH, FAR FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank a just person. Settle into your breath. This time, look for fairness from someone who owed you nothing: a person outside your circle, of another faith or background, who held the rules level when it would have been easy to tilt them. An official who processed your papers honestly. A referee who called it straight against the home crowd. A landlord who gave back the whole deposit. Notice exactly what they did, and what it might have cost them. Then thank them, if you can reach them, naming the fair thing. If you can't, say their name and the thanks quietly now. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Hijrah. The Prophet sends companions to Abyssinia, the first emigration in Islam, to a king who, he says, rules so that no one is wronged. Today's word.
Your line: a just king. Today, when you have a little power over someone, a decision, a grade, a turn, use it so that no one is wronged. Day seven hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims know this as the emigration to Abyssinia (al-Habashah), told in sirah lessons as the community's first hijrah, and the Negus is remembered with honor for sheltering them.

original.note: Arabic: emigration, leaving one place for another; Ibn Ishaq calls the journey to Abyssinia the first hijrah in Islam.

trapdoor: what you thought: the early Muslims fled to wherever they could.
what it means: the Prophet chose a place for its justice, sending his own daughter to a Christian king.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq's 'a land of truthfulness' and 'the first hijrah'; Umm Salamah's report in Musnad Ahmad of being safe in their faith.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the first emigration to Abyssinia: a king under whom none is wronged, a land of truthfulness; Uthman and Ruqayyah among the emigrants)
Musnad Ahmad 1740 (Umm Salamah: in Abyssinia, the best of neighbors; safe in their religion)

notes: The Prophet's words about the king are paraphrased from Ibn Ishaq; confirm.
'The first emigration in Islam' is attributed to Ibn Ishaq; confirm the wording there.
Musnad Ahmad 1740 number cited from memory (Umm Salamah's long report); confirm. The same report carries Ja'far's speech (day 743).
Umm Salamah's presence on the first emigration vs. a later party: the script says only that she went too. Confirm.

The Negus is described as a Christian ruling a Christian land, with no claim about his later faith; Muslim tradition holds he later accepted Islam (the Prophet prayed the funeral prayer for him). A Keeper may want this noted on a later day.
Editor: cut the unsourced geography 'on the far shore of the Red Sea' from the hook (and its note); 'across the sea' kept.

Auditor: reworked the practice so it no longer repeats the 'thank someone who believed in you / protected you' practices of days 728 and 735 (now: fairness from someone outside your circle, echoing the Negus); trimmed the teach's closing, which restated the 'first hijrah' point twice.
